entities.sub: Sec. 1102 of Division M (Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024) of S. 2226, 118th Congress, as engrossed in the Senate 27 July 2023 - 'Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena'

claims.text: The operative body of Sec. 1102 was NOT retrieved and remains unread. Six independent primary vehicles for the text were attempted and every one of them was defeated by the same failure mode - the fetch tool's extraction ceiling, which lands somewhere between roughly 92,000 and 145,000 characters depending on the density of the document, and which always truncates from the start of the file forward. The attempts and the exact point each one died: (1) govinfo HTML of the engrossed bill, BILLS-118s2226es.htm, cut at 129,012 characters, still inside Division A; (2) the Senate Intelligence Committee's own posted PDF of the engrossed bill, cut at 103,001 characters, still inside the bill's table of contents, with the Sec. 1102 TOC line reached but no body; (3) the Senate Intelligence Committee's HTML rendering of Division M, cut at 122,645 characters at Title VIII, Sec. 801; (4) govinfo HTML of S. 2103 as reported, cut at 144,209 characters mid-sentence in Title VII; (5) the govinfo PDF of S. 2103 as reported, cut at 91,997 characters at page 67 of the print; (6) the Congressional Record granule containing the full Division M text as SA 1053, PDF cut at 132,368 characters at Sec. 804 and the HTML twin of the same granule cut at 138,797 characters inside Title IX, roughly two printed pages short of Title XI. There is no page-range or byte-range access to any of these, and the Congressional Record link service resolves every page from S3628 through S3642 to the same single granule, so no later starting point exists.

Both the Senate Intelligence Committee's posting of the engrossed text and the Congressional Record print of SA 1053 carry the identical Title XI table of contents, and Title XI--Other Matters of Division M contains exactly two sections and no others: 'Sec. 1101. Modification of reporting requirement for All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office.' and 'Sec. 1102. Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

Mark Warner as amendment SA 1053 to S. 2226 and printed in full in the Congressional Record for 26 July 2023 at pages S3628-S3642. The internal table of contents of the SA 1053 print uses Division M section numbering - Sec. 1101 and Sec. 1102 - not the S. 2103 reported numbering, which means the Congressional Record print of SA 1053 is a page-addressable primary copy of the same text the board node cites. claims.text: RENUMBERING AND ATTRITION BETWEEN COMMITTEE AND FLOOR. In S. 2103 as reported by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 22 June 2023, Title XI--Other Matters contained four sections: 'Sec. 1101. Modification of reporting requirement for All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office.'; 'Sec. 1102. Modifications to notification on the provision of defense sensitive [support]'; 'Sec. 1103. Modification of congressional oversight of special access programs.'; and 'Sec. 1104. Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' The engrossed Division M carries only the first and the last of these, renumbered 1101 and 1102. Two provisions were therefore dropped between committee and the Senate-passed text, and one of the two dropped provisions was a direct amendment to the congressional oversight regime for special access programs. That is a soft joint the board did not previously have: the same intelligence committee that wrote the UAP funding limitation also wrote a special access program oversight amendment alongside it, and only the funding limitation survived to the floor text.
claims.source: S. 2103, Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, as reported 22 June 2023 - https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s2103rs/html/BILLS-118s2103rs.htm (table of contents, Title XI) ; compared against Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, 'Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Division M of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, as passed by the Senate on July 27, 2023', 9 August 2023 - https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/2023/08/09/legislation-intelligence-authorization-act-fiscal-year-2024-division-m-national-defense/ (posted PDF: https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/sites-default-files-legislation-bills-118s2226es.pdf)

claims.text: Because the engrossed body was never read, the specific elements the board attributes to Sec. 1102 - a 60-day contractor notification deadline running to the Director of AARO, a 180-day deadline to make material available, the phrase 'non-earth origin or exotic', and the phrase 'assessment, analysis, and inspection' - remain corroborated ONLY by DefenseScoop's 27 June 2023 report, and that report is describing Sec. 1104 of S. 2103 as reported, not Sec. 1102 of Division M as engrossed. The reporter quotes the following fragments inside quotation marks: a mandate on any person currently or formerly under contract with the federal government that 'has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the' government relating to UAP 'that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access' to notify the AARO Director within 60 days of enactment; and, no later than 180 days after passage, to make 'all such material and information' and 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic [UAP] material' available to AARO for 'assessment, analysis, and inspection'. The bracketed [UAP] is the reporter's insertion, which is itself a sign that the quoted string is being edited. Treat these as reported fragments of the REPORTED text, not as verified text of the ENGROSSED section.
claims.source: Brandi Vincent, 'Senate's intelligence authorization bill questions reverse engineering of government-recovered UAPs', DefenseScoop, 27 June 2023 - https://defensescoop.com/2023/06/27/senates-intelligence-authorization-bill-questions-reverse-engineering-of-government-recovered-uaps/

claims.text: ENACTED SUCCESSOR IDENTIFIED AND CONFIRMED FROM A PRIMARY SOURCE. The provision was enacted as Section 7343 of Division G of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Pub. L. 118-31. The Explanatory Statement to accompany the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, printed in the Congressional Record by Sen. Warner on 14 December 2023 and given the same effect as a joint explanatory statement of a conference committee, states verbatim: 'Section 7343 of the Act provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area. Section 7343 is also intended to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist. Section 7343 further provides a limitation regarding independent research and development funding to ensure that certain indirect expenses are prohibited.' The explanatory statement says nothing whatever about a 60-day contractor turn-in, a list of non-earth origin material, or a make-available mandate to AARO.
claims.source: Explanatory Statement on the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, printed by Sen. Warner, Congressional Record, Vol. 169, No. 206 (14 December 2023), pp. S5990-S5991 - https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CREC-2023-12-14/html/CREC-2023-12-14-pt1-PgS5990.htm

claims.text: A SECOND, PARALLEL ENACTED PROVISION EXISTS IN DIVISION A. The table of contents of the statute compilation of Pub. L. 118-31 shows 'Sec. 1687. Limitation on use of funds for certain unreported programs.' in Division A, Title XVI, distinct from and in addition to Sec. 7343 in Division G. The board should carry both: the FY2024 NDAA enacted two separate UAP funding-limitation provisions, one in the defence division and one in the intelligence division.
claims.source: Statute compilation of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 (Pub. L. 118-31), table of contents - https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/COMPS-17632/pdf/COMPS-17632.pdf

claims.text: THE ONLY PART OF THE ENACTED FAMILY THAT COULD BE READ VERBATIM CONTAINS NONE OF THE THREE DISPUTED ELEMENTS. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel sets out subsections (b) and (c) of Pub. L. 118-31, div. A, title XVI, Sec. 1687 as a statutory note under 50 U.S.C. 3373, under the heading 'Limitation Regarding Independent Research and Development'. The full text of subsection (b) as set out reads: 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Subsection (c) then defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus the two intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' as the Senate majority and minority leaders and the Speaker and House minority leader. There is no 60-day deadline, no 180-day deadline, no 'non-earth origin or exotic' language, and no reference to AARO anywhere in the enacted text that OLRC chose to print. The sentence also carries a drafting error that survived into law - 'is made available the appropriate congressional committees', with the preposition 'to' missing - which is itself evidence that this is the enacted text and not a paraphrase. NOTE THE LIMIT OF THIS FINDING: it establishes what is in Sec. 1687(b)-(c), not what is in Sec. 7343, whose body was not retrieved. OLRC set out only subsections (b) and (c) of Sec. 1687 and set out no part of Sec. 7343 as a note anywhere the board has checked.

entities.sub: 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight', added by Pub. L. 100-180 Sec. 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987; last amended 2001

claims.text: The waiver authority reads verbatim, as in effect on 20 August 2026: '(e)(1) The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis. (2) If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' The waiver is a waiver of INCLUSION IN A REPORT, not a waiver of disclosure - the withheld information and a written justification must still travel to twelve named seats.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: The recipient set is fixed by subsection (g) verbatim: 'In this section, the term "defense committees" means- (1) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and (2) the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House of Representatives.' Six committee entities, each contributing a chairman and a ranking minority member, gives the twelve-seat notification group the board already tracks.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: MATERIAL NEW FINDING - THE REPORTS THE WAIVER ATTACHES TO HAVE LARGELY SUNSET. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel carries a statutory note under 10 U.S.C. 119 headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' which reads verbatim: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The annual special access program report under 119(a) and the new-program notice and justification report under 119(b) therefore terminated as statutory requirements on 31 December 2021. After that date the only report to which the 119(e)(1) waiver can attach is the 119(c) report on a planned classification change or public declassification announcement. This reshapes the board's question: for activity after 31 December 2021 there may be no 119(a) or 119(b) report in existence to waive information out of, which would make the absence of any 119(e)(2) delivery unsurprising rather than suspicious for that window - while for the period 1988 through 2021 the reports were mandatory and the waiver machinery was live.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: Section 119 has not been amended since 2001. The source credit runs Pub. L. 100-180 (1987), Pub. L. 101-510 (1990), Pub. L. 104-106 (1996), Pub. L. 106-65 (1999), Pub. L. 107-107 (2001), and stops. The Senate Intelligence Committee's Sec. 1103 of S. 2103 as reported in June 2023, 'Modification of congressional oversight of special access programs', would have been the first amendment in twenty-two years; it does not appear in the Senate-passed Division M and Section 119 as it stands today shows no 2023 or 2024 amendment.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim ; and S. 2103, Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, as reported 22 June 2023 - https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-118s2103rs/html/BILLS-118s2103rs.htm

claims.text: Neither Sec. 1687 nor Sec. 7343 of Pub. L. 118-31 is set out as a statutory note under 10 U.S.C. 119. The notes carried under Section 119 are limited to the 1990 effective-date note, the termination-of-reporting note, and the 1987 initial-reports note. Whatever the FY2024 NDAA did to UAP funding, it did not attach itself to the Section 119 oversight architecture in the U.S. Code.

entities.sub: The designation of an unacknowledged special access program as 'waived' under the Secretary of Defense's 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) authority

claims.text: VERDICT ON THE BOARD'S QUESTION: the waiver has been exercised, and the Department of Defense says so in a currently effective, publicly released instruction - but no public document identifies a single specific instance, a count, a date, a program, or any connection to unidentified anomalous phenomena. DoD Instruction 5205.11, effective 12 September 2024, paragraph 1.2.f, states verbatim: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.' This is not a hypothetical authority described in the abstract; the rest of the instruction is written around an existing population of such programs.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: THE STRONGEST SINGLE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT THE POPULATION IS NON-EMPTY IS A RECURRING REVIEW REQUIREMENT. DoDI 5205.11 requires that in its annual review the Special Access Program Oversight Committee - chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense - shall assess, among four listed items, '(d) All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' A standing annual agenda item to decide whether waived programs should REMAIN waived is only drafted if waived programs exist. This is a 2024 document, so the finding is current, not historical.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: The Department's own definition, from the DoDI 5205.11 glossary, verbatim: 'waived SAP - A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' And, adjacent to it: 'unacknowledged SAP - A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A waived SAP is therefore a proper subset of the unacknowledged SAPs, distinguished precisely by the exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: Administrative plumbing specific to waived programs exists in the same instruction, which again indicates live use rather than dormant authority. Footnote 5 reads verbatim: 'CA and OA SAPCO Directors may delegate AAA for non-waived SAPs to the DoD Component's SAPCO staff. AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee.' Footnote 6 reads verbatim: 'DoD SAPCO will coordinate on PARs for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs.' A department does not write delegation rules and a judicial-access coordination rule for an empty set.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: THE PUBLIC TAXONOMY HAS BEEN NARROWING. DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy', was reissued effective 12 September 2024 and cancels the 1 July 2010 version. The full public text of the 2024 directive - purpose, applicability, policy, all thirteen responsibility assignments, the governance section, the complete glossary and the reference list - contains no occurrence of the words 'waived' or 'unacknowledged' at all. The directive that used to define the waived category no longer mentions it; the taxonomy now survives publicly only in the subordinate instruction, DoDI 5205.11. Anyone checking only the directive would conclude the category no longer exists.
claims.source: DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy', effective 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/portals/54/documents/dd/issuances/dodd/520507p.pdf

claims.text: HISTORICAL CORROBORATION FROM A CONGRESSIONALLY CHARTERED COMMISSION. The Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (1997), Chapter II, states verbatim: 'Among black programs, further distinction is made for "waived" programs, considered to be so sensitive that they are exempt from standard reporting requirements to the Congress. The chairperson, ranking member, and, on occasion, other members and staff of relevant Congressional committees are notified only orally of the existence of these programs.' The same passage gives the surrounding population: 'There are approximately 150 DoD-approved SAPs (the exact number is classified and others have been created but not yet formally approved), down from 200 in the late 1980s, and roughly 300 SCI compartments, compared with an estimated 800 in the late 1980s.' The Commission gives no number for the waived subset. The phrase 'notified only orally' is the operationally important one: it describes a practice under which the 119(e)(2) delivery leaves no paper.
claims.source: Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (the Moynihan Commission), S. Doc. 105-2, 1997, Chapter II, as mirrored by the Federation of American Scientists - https://sgp.fas.org/library/moynihan/chap2.html

claims.text: GAO HAS DESCRIBED THE WAIVER MECHANISM BUT HAS NEVER PUBLICLY REPORTED AN INSTANCE OF ITS USE. GAO/NSIAD-93-78, the unclassified summary of a classified report, describes the mechanism verbatim: 'Section 119, 10 U.S. Code, enacted in 1987, requires DOD to submit annual reports to the congressional defense committees on special access programs. Under the law, the Secretary of Defense may waive the requirement that certain information on special access programs be included in the annual report if he determines that the inclusion would adversely affect national security. However, he must provide the excluded information to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' The report then never returns to the subject. Its findings on waivers are about a different thing entirely - 'DOD used waivers and exemptions to limit review, documentation, and reporting requirements' refers to Defense Acquisition Board reviews, competition requirements and Selected Acquisition Reports, not to Section 119(e). Do not let these two senses of 'waiver' be conflated on the board.
claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-93-78, 'Defense Acquisition: Oversight of Special Access Programs Has Increased', 21 December 1992 - https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-93-78.pdf

claims.text: The earlier GAO report in the same series, GAO/NSIAD-89-133, covering the period immediately after Section 119 took effect and prepared at the request of Rep. Barbara Boxer, examines DoD compliance with special access program oversight requirements in detail and does not mention the Section 119(e) waiver authority at all. Its only reference to waived requirements is to DoD Directive 5205.7's January 1989 revision requiring 'listings by the responsible program officer of all DOD regulations for which compliance has been waived' - again a different mechanism.
claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-89-133, 'Special Access Programs: DOD Is Strengthening Compliance With Oversight Requirements', 4 May 1989 - https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-89-133.pdf

claims.text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. None of the four is a public document class. There is no statutory requirement anywhere in Section 119 to report the NUMBER of waivers exercised, the fact that any waiver was exercised, or an aggregate count, to anyone outside those twelve seats. The absence of a public instance is therefore fully explained by the design of the mechanism and is NOT evidence of concealment beyond what the statute itself authorises.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim ; DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf ; Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (the Moynihan Commission), S. Doc. 105-2, 1997, Chapter II, as mirrored by the Federation of American Scientists - https://sgp.fas.org/library/moynihan/chap2.html

claims.text: NO UAP-SPECIFIC EXERCISE OF THE 119(e)(1) WAIVER WAS FOUND IN ANY PUBLIC DOCUMENT. Searches across GAO's special access program series, DoD Inspector General audits and evaluations, Congressional Research Service products, and the Senate and House Armed Services Committee document sets returned no document in which a waived special access program is linked to unidentified anomalous phenomena, and no document in which any specific exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver - UAP or otherwise - is identified, dated, counted or described. The DoD Inspector General's public catalogue for special access programs consists of external peer reviews and quality control reviews of the service audit agencies' SAP audit work, plus a series of entries titled only 'CLASSIFIED REPORT (Classified)'; none addresses congressional reporting under Section 119.
claims.source: Negative result of searches restricted to gao.gov, dodig.mil, crsreports.congress.gov, armed-services.senate.gov, armedservices.house.gov and govinfo.gov during this pass

entities.sub: The persons entitled to notice of, and access to, a waived DoD special access program

claims.text: THE STATUTORY GROUP AND THE DEPARTMENT'S GROUP ARE NOT THE SAME, AND THE DEPARTMENT'S IS WIDER. The statute, 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2), names only 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' - twelve seats across six committee entities, and no staff. DoD Instruction 5205.11, paragraph 7.2.a.(3), states verbatim: 'Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' The Department therefore adds two staff categories the statute does not name, and extends the group to the two intelligence committees, which Section 119(g) does not include. Whether that is a lawful gloss or an administrative expansion is a live question the board can put on the record.
claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight' (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim ; and DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: The exclusion of ordinary committee members from waived programs is stated flatly. DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.b reads verbatim: 'Members of Congress assigned to the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to all DoD SAPs within the respective committee's SAP oversight jurisdiction, except for waived programs as described previously. The intelligence committees are authorized access only to those DoD SAPs designated by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense as intelligence or intelligence related.'
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: Professional staff members are cut out of waived programs entirely. DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.c.(1) reads verbatim: 'One professional staff member for both the majority and the minority party of the defense and intelligence committees may be granted access to all non-waived SAPs within the respective committee's SAP oversight jurisdiction.' Paragraph 7.2.d applies the same limit to non-committee members: 'Members of Congress and professional staff members not assigned to the defense or intelligence committees may be granted access to non-waived DoD SAPs by the Director, DoD SAPCO following consultation with the respective chamber of Congress chair and ranking defense committee members.'
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: THE BUDGET PAPER FOR A WAIVED PROGRAM GOES TO STAFF, NOT TO MEMBERS. DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.h reads verbatim: 'The DoD will conform to all congressional reporting requirements. The DoD will submit to the congressional defense and intelligence committees such additional materials as are requested by the committees and are within the jurisdiction of each committee. Justification materials for waived programs will be presented only to the committee staff directors.' This is a distinct and narrower channel than the 119(e)(2) delivery to chairs and ranking members, and it means the written justification material for a waived program is routed to two staff directors per committee rather than to the twelve statutory seats.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: Umbrella access does not carry down into waived compartments. DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a.(2) reads verbatim: 'When a member of Congress or a professional staff member is given access to a SAP umbrella, that member of Congress or professional staff member will also be given access to all compartments and sub-compartments that fall under the respective SAP umbrella, with the exception of waived sub-compartments as described in Paragraph 7.2.a.(3).' A waived sub-compartment can therefore sit inside an umbrella a member is fully read into, invisibly to that member.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: GAO's own access is gated through the same two seats. DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.g provides that GAO access runs through 'the chairman and ranking defense committee members, unless the GAO is already tasked with a SAP-related action in existing legislation.' This is the structural reason GAO's published special access program work has never been able to report on the waiver's use.
claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: The historical practice of the notification was oral. The Moynihan Commission recorded in 1997 that for waived programs 'the chairperson, ranking member, and, on occasion, other members and staff of relevant Congressional committees are notified only orally of the existence of these programs.' If that practice persisted, then the 119(e)(2) delivery of 'the information ... and the justification for the waiver' generates no artefact that can later be produced, subpoenaed, archived or discovered - which is the single most consequential fact on this node.

findings: QUESTION 1 IS NOT CLOSED. The operative body of Sec. 1102 of Division M of S. 2226 as engrossed was not retrieved. Six primary vehicles were tried - the govinfo HTML of the engrossed bill, the Senate Intelligence Committee's posted PDF of the engrossed bill, the Committee's HTML rendering of Division M, the govinfo HTML and PDF of S. 2103 as reported, and both the PDF and HTML of the Congressional Record granule carrying the full division as SA 1053 - and every one was cut off by the same extraction ceiling before reaching Title XI. The closest approach was the Congressional Record HTML granule, which died inside Title IX, roughly two printed pages short of the target.

The 60-day deadline, the 'non-earth origin or exotic' language and the make-available-to-AARO mandate therefore remain UNVERIFIED against any bill text. They rest on a single DefenseScoop report of 27 June 2023 which is describing Sec. 1104 of S. 2103 as reported, not Sec. 1102 of Division M as engrossed, and which brackets its own insertion into one of the quoted phrases. The board should downgrade, not upgrade, its confidence in these three elements until the body text is read.

The section heading and placement are now verified against a SECOND independent primary copy. Title XI--Other Matters of Division M contains exactly two sections, Sec. 1101 and Sec. 1102, in both the Senate Intelligence Committee's posting of the engrossed text and the Congressional Record print of SA 1053.

A better citation vehicle has been identified for future retrieval: the full Division M text was submitted by Sen. Warner as SA 1053 and printed in the Congressional Record for 26 July 2023 at pages S3628-S3642, govinfo granule CREC-2023-07-26-pt1-PgS3627-2, using Division M section numbering. Any tool with page-level or byte-range access should be pointed here rather than at the 2,400-page engrossed bill.

NEW SOFT JOINT DISCOVERED. Between the Senate Intelligence Committee's reported bill of 22 June 2023 and the Senate-passed Division M of 27 July 2023, Title XI shed two sections: reported Sec. 1102, on notification for the provision of defense sensitive support, and reported Sec. 1103, 'Modification of congressional oversight of special access programs'. The UAP funding limitation survived, renumbered from 1104 to 1102; the special access program oversight amendment did not. Ten U.S.C. 119 has not been amended since 2001, so that dropped section would have been the first change to the SAP oversight statute in twenty-two years.

The enacted successor is Section 7343 of Division G of Pub. L. 118-31, confirmed from the explanatory statement Sen. Warner printed in the Congressional Record on 14 December 2023, which describes it as providing funding limitations 'because of perceptions of insufficient transparency', as intended to 'expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist', and as further providing an independent research and development funding limitation. A parallel provision, Sec. 1687 'Limitation on use of funds for certain unreported programs', was enacted separately in Division A, Title XVI of the same public law.

The only part of the enacted family that could be read verbatim - Sec. 1687(b) and (c), set out as a statutory note under 50 U.S.C. 3373 - contains none of the three disputed elements. It conditions the allowability of independent research and development funding as an indirect expense on the material and information being made available to the congressional defence and intelligence committees and to congressional leadership, and it stops there. No 60 days, no 180 days, no 'non-earth origin or exotic', no AARO. This is a limit on what Sec. 1687 says, not a finding about what Sec. 7343 says.

QUESTION 2 IS CLOSED IN THE AFFIRMATIVE, AT THE LEVEL OF THE MECHANISM. The Department of Defense states in a currently effective, publicly released instruction that the waiver category is populated and under recurring review. DoDI 5205.11 of 12 September 2024 provides that the Secretary 'may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" ... pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code', defines a waived SAP in its glossary as one 'for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security', and requires the Special Access Program Oversight Committee to assess in its annual review 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status'. A standing annual agenda item to reconsider whether waived programs should stay waived cannot be written for an empty set.

QUESTION 2 IS NOT CLOSED AT THE LEVEL OF THE INSTANCE. No public document identifies a single specific exercise of the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) waiver - not a date, not a program, not a count, not an aggregate. No public document links a waived special access program to unidentified anomalous phenomena. GAO's special access program series describes the mechanism (NSIAD-93-78, 1992) but never reports an instance; the earlier report in the same series (NSIAD-89-133, 1989) does not mention it at all; the DoD Inspector General's public special access program catalogue consists of peer reviews of service audit agencies and entries titled only 'CLASSIFIED REPORT (Classified)'.

THE ABSENCE IS FULLY EXPLAINED BY DESIGN, NOT BY ANOMALY - and the board should record that, because it removes an inference it might otherwise be tempted to draw. Section 119 imposes no requirement to report the number of waivers, the fact of a waiver, or an aggregate, to anyone beyond the twelve statutory seats. GAO's own access to special access programs is gated through the chairman and ranking members of the defence committees under DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.g. And the Moynihan Commission recorded in 1997 that notification for waived programs was given 'only orally', which means the delivery required by 119(e)(2) may historically have produced no artefact at all.

MATERIAL STRUCTURAL FINDING ON THE STATUTE. A statutory note under 10 U.S.C. 119 records that the annual reports required by subsections (a) and (b) terminated, effective 31 December 2021, under section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328. After that date the only surviving report to which the 119(e)(1) waiver can attach is the 119(c) report on a planned classification change or public declassification. Yet DoD's September 2024 instruction still designates waived SAPs 'pursuant to Section 119'. The Department is invoking a waiver of reporting requirements two of which Congress allowed to lapse. That tension is new to the board and is the sharpest single question this pass produced.

THE DEPARTMENT'S NOTIFICATION GROUP IS WIDER THAN THE STATUTE'S. Section 119(e)(2) names only the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the six defence committees. DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a.(3) authorises access to waived SAPs for 'the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense AND intelligence committees'. The Department adds two staff categories the statute does not name and extends the group to two committees Section 119(g) does not list. Separately, paragraph 7.2.h routes justification materials for waived programs 'only to the committee staff directors' - a narrower and different channel from the statutory delivery to members.

THE PUBLIC TAXONOMY IS SHRINKING. DoD Directive 5205.07 was reissued on 12 September 2024, cancelling the 2010 version. The full public text of the new directive - including its complete glossary - contains no occurrence of 'waived' or 'unacknowledged'. The category now appears publicly only in the subordinate instruction. A reader checking the governing directive alone would conclude the waived category no longer exists.

The verbatim text of Section 7343 of Division G of Pub. L. 118-31, the enacted successor. BLOCKER: same ceiling. Division G sits at roughly Statutes at Large page 1062 onward of a 1,200-page public law; the govinfo PLAW and COMPS files, the enrolled bill, and the Senate Intelligence Committee's posting of Division G all truncate before reaching it - the Committee's Division G page got as far as the CIA sexual-harassment reporting provisions in Title III before cutting. Whether the enacted Sec. 7343 retains the 60-day contractor notification, the 180-day make-available deadline, the 'non-earth origin or exotic' list, or any reference to AARO. Because the verbatim text of neither the engrossed Sec. 1102 nor the enacted Sec. 7343 was read, the board cannot yet say whether these elements were enacted, narrowed, or dropped. The one adjacent provision that WAS read verbatim - Sec. 1687(b)-(c) as set out under 50 U.S.C. 3373 - contains none of them, but Sec. 1687 is a different section in a different division and cannot stand in for Sec. 7343.

Any specific, dated, identified exercise of the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) waiver. BLOCKER: no public document class exists in which such an instance would appear. The statute requires no public reporting of waiver use; the delivery under 119(e)(2) runs to twelve members and, per the Moynihan Commission, has historically been oral; GAO's access is gated through the defence committee chairs and ranking members under DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.g; and the DoD Inspector General's relevant products are published only as titles. This is a genuine negative and should be recorded as such rather than left as an open question.

The number of waived DoD special access programs at any date. The Moynihan Commission gave a total of approximately 150 DoD-approved SAPs in 1997 but explicitly gave no figure for the waived subset, and no later public source found in this pass gives one.

The verbatim text of Sec. 1103 of S. 2103 as reported, 'Modification of congressional oversight of special access programs' - the provision that would have amended 10 U.S.C. 119 and that did not survive into Division M. BLOCKER: same extraction ceiling; it sits in Title XI of the reported bill, immediately before the UAP funding limitation, and every retrieval of that bill died in Title VII. What it proposed to change, and why it was dropped between committee and floor, is now a specific and answerable question for the next pass.

The section-by-section analysis of Sec. 1104 in Senate Report 118-59, which would give the Intelligence Committee's own official description of the provision and would upgrade the corroboration from journalism to a congressional committee report. The report was retrieved in full from govinfo but the tool persisted it as a single-line JSON blob whose long lines the grep tool refuses to print, so the relevant passage could not be read out.
